Having to pay for digital damage is the most absurd bullshit. Seriously. This is also why I think piracy laws are goddamn stupid - The companies in question can only argue that there's THEORETICAL damage being done, because it's a "Lost Sale". However, all evidence is to the contrary - The games with the most draconian DRM and that don't get cracked. . . Don't see any projected change in sales. I mean, after all, those people were ALL going to buy your game, right? RIGHT? Fucking wrong.

What's my point? Digital damages are bullshit - There's literally no such thing as far as digitally downloadable content is concerned. The people who think you have a good product, feel that it's priced appropriately for them and don't have a personal vendetta against you for being douchenozzles will purchase it. The people on the opposite end of any of these spectrums will very likely not purchase it - These are the ACTUAL lost sales, because those people were actually contemplating giving you money, whereas someone with merely passing interest who wouldn't give a fuck otherwise aren't going to buy your product. You've lost nothing by them "stealing" your product, it cost you nothing for them to take it because the alternative is not "They would be forced to buy it", it's "They wouldn't play and wouldn't be interested." Thus, digital damages are horseshit, and fuck all of the companies that enforce them (To varying degrees naturally).

While I agree that "digital damages" are bullshit... It did cost something to them. It cost bandwidth and server resources to serve the file to the individual. Not that those numbers are not negligible in the long run; however, making generalized sweeping statements is what gets us into the problem we're in right now.

No, it didn't cost them anything because of amortization of that connection. To begin with, your bandwidth has always been charged for how big of a pipe you have, not what flows through. They can't make that argument, nor should they. As for the computing resources (Which boils down to power draw), data centers are designed, and have hardware specification to deal with their peak activity - This means that any single user doesn't make much of an impact on the power draw, and then you have to average that out with ALL of your connections AND you idle power draw (servers are really, really fragile to being turned off and on. You basically never turn them off unless you have a planned reason to do so, or it's an emergency). Effectively, this means that the one thief has a non-existent impact on the operations of the data center financially. Individual users cost them nothing, it's the culmination of all of their users during peak usage that costs them - That's the reason they have that hardware, for the 6 hours of the day that they get hit hard. This is why subscription models are so cheap, you as an individual basically cost them nothing. This is also why the F2P model is so profitable, despite a grand majority of people never spending a red cent on games that have that model. Those individual people "Consuming Bandwidth and server resources" cost them such a negligible amount that they literally do not give a fuck about them playing for free forever. Thus, bandwidth and server resources is an argument that I have not to date seen a company make, and I doubt they ever will make it, due to fear of being laughed out of the room.

So yes. It cost them nothing.

Sucks, but I doubt they would do this without reason. No, I'm not a Sony shill. Where I work, we get disputes all of the time on fraudulent Playstation charges, and Sony very rarely fights when we submit these for charge back. When they do fight us, it usually ends up being the customer. I wouldn't be surprised if it turns out the fraudulent purchases were done by someone else in this users' household using their console or IP address, which is why Sony is saying they won't assist them in refunding these charges.

More importantly, the article claims:

In the meantime, they added a device to my account, a PS Vita. Unlike a PS3 or PS4, a PS Vita can't be removed from the account by Web, it can only be deactivated from the device itself.

It actually can be removed by going to account.sonyentertainmentnetwork.com and removing it.

The guy also claims:

The email wasn't opened, nor had any odd devices accessed my email account, but another message less than a minute later confirmed the email change. Yep. While I was sleeping, someone locked me out of my own account.

...which makes it even more likely his roommate, or someone his roommate invited over did this.

The next part:

The agent passed the buck. They explained that in order to issue a refund, I needed to cancel the dispute with PayPal. Essentially, PayPal had taken the money back from Sony, and I needed to have PayPal release it so Sony could hand it back to me.

This is part of the charge back process, and once initiated, time needs to pass to work this out. When your payment source (PayPal) charges something back to the merchant, the merchant has 45 days to respond if they wish to challenge the charge back. If PayPal were to "cancel" the dispute, Sony could still challenge the charge back and take the money from PayPal, who is then the one left holding the bill. So PayPal won't cancel the charge back until the time period of at least 45 days has passed.

The next part:

I asked what would happen if I issued a chargeback at the debit card level, and the agent explained matter-of-factly that my account would be banned until I paid the $75 in fraudulent charges.

They do this because people abuse the charge back process. They buy games they want, play the shit out of them, then charge it back 2 months later and claim fraud. Without a policy like this in place, Sony would simply lose money and not know who is scamming them and who is truly a victim of fraud.

The proper steps would have been to report this error to Sony first, and if they were unable to resolve the issue, THEN report it to PayPal or the bank that issues your debit card.
That's a bunch of crap, so he has to pay for what Sony should have been protecting in the first place.
